# cranelift_bforest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-bforest/0.106.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cranelift_bforest/index.html

## Expand description

A forest of B+-trees.

This crate provides a data structures representing a set of small ordered sets or maps. It is implemented as a forest of B+-trees all allocating nodes out of the same pool.

**These are not general purpose data structures that are somehow magically faster that the
standard library’s  BTreeSet and BTreeMap types.**

The tradeoffs are different:

- Keys and values are expected to be small and copyable. We optimize for 32-bit types.
- A comparator object is used to compare keys, allowing smaller “context free” keys.
- Empty trees have a very small 32-bit footprint.
- All the trees in a forest can be cleared in constant time.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- B-tree mapping from`K`to`V`.
- A position in a`Map`used to navigate and modify the ordered map.
- Memory pool for a forest of`Map`instances.
- An iterator visiting the key-value pairs of a`Map`.
- B-tree representing an ordered set of`K`s using`C`for comparing elements.
- A position in a`Set`used to navigate and modify the ordered set.
- Memory pool for a forest of`Set`instances.
- An iterator visiting the elements of a`Set`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- Key comparator.

# cranelift_control - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-control/0.106.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cranelift_control/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cranelift-control)Cranelift Control

This is the home of the control plane of chaos mode, a compilation feature
intended to be turned on for certain fuzz targets. When the feature is
turned off, as is normally the case, [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html) will be a zero-sized
type and optimized away.

While the feature is turned on, the struct [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html)
provides functionality to tap into pseudo-randomness at specific locations
in the code. It may be used for targeted fuzzing of compiler internals,
e.g. manipulate heuristic optimizations, clobber undefined register bits
etc.

There are two ways to acquire a [ControlPlane](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html):

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.arbitrary)for the real deal
- [default](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlPlane.html#method.default)for an “empty” control plane which always returns default values

[§](https://docs.rs#fuel-limit)Fuel Limit

Controls the number of mutations or optimizations that the compiler will perform before stopping.

When a perturbation introduced by chaos mode triggers a bug, it may not be immediately clear which of the introduced perturbations was the trigger. The fuel limit can then be used to binary-search for the trigger. It limits the number of perturbations introduced by the control plane. The fuel limit will typically be set with a command line argument passed to a fuzz target. For example:

```
cargo fuzz run --features chaos $TARGET -- --fuel=16
```

# cranelift_entity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-entity/0.106.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cranelift_entity/index.html

## Expand description

Array-based data structures using densely numbered entity references as mapping keys.

This crate defines a number of data structures based on arrays. The arrays are not indexed by
`usize` as usual, but by *entity references* which are integers wrapped in new-types. This has
a couple advantages:

- Improved type safety. The various map and set types accept a specific key type, so there is no confusion about the meaning of an array index, as there is with plain arrays.
- Smaller indexes. The normal `usize`index is often 64 bits which is way too large for most purposes. The entity reference types can be smaller, allowing for more compact data structures.

The `EntityRef` trait should be implemented by types to be used as indexed. The `entity_impl!`
macro provides convenient defaults for types wrapping `u32` which is common.

- `PrimaryMap`
- `SecondaryMap`
- `SparseMap`
- `EntitySet`
- `EntityList`- `Vec`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Compact representation of`Option<T>`for types with a reserved value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Macro which provides the common implementation of a 32-bit entity reference.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A slice mapping`K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- A small list of entity references allocated from a pool.
- A set of`K`for densely indexed entity references.
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- Iterate over all keys in order.
- A memory pool for storing lists of`T`.
- A primary mapping`K -> V`allocating dense entity references.
- A mapping`K -> V`for densely indexed entity references.
- A sparse mapping of entity references.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- A type wrapping a small integer index should implement`EntityRef`so it can be used as the key of an`SecondaryMap`or`SparseMap`.
- Trait for extracting keys from values stored in a`SparseMap`.

# MachBuffer in cranelift_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-codegen/^0.106.2/struct.MachBuffer.html

`pub struct MachBuffer<I: VCodeInst> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A buffer of output to be produced, fixed up, and then emitted to a CodeSink in bulk.

This struct uses `SmallVec`s to support small-ish function bodies without
any heap allocation. As such, it will be several kilobytes large. This is
likely fine as long as it is stack-allocated for function emission then
thrown away; but beware if many buffer objects are retained persistently.

#### pub fn [add_uncond_branch](https://docs.rs#method.add_uncond_branch)(
    &mut self,
    start: [CodeOffset](https://docs.rs/binemit/type.CodeOffset.html),
    end: [CodeOffset](https://docs.rs/binemit/type.CodeOffset.html),
    target: [MachLabel](https://docs.rs/struct.MachLabel.html)
)

Inform the buffer of an unconditional branch at the given offset,
targetting the given label. May be used to optimize branches.
The last added label-use must correspond to this branch.
This must be called when the current offset is equal to `start`; i.e.,
before actually emitting the branch. This implies that for a branch that
uses a label and is eligible for optimizations by the MachBuffer, the
proper sequence is:

- Call `use_label_at_offset()`to emit the fixup record.
- Call `add_uncond_branch()`to make note of the branch.
- Emit the bytes for the branch’s machine code.

Additional requirement: no labels may be bound between `start` and `end`
(exclusive on both ends).

[source](https://docs.rs/src/cranelift_codegen/machinst/buffer.rs.html#1663-1681)

#### pub fn [add_stack_map](https://docs.rs#method.add_stack_map)(&mut self, extent: StackMapExtent, stack_map: [StackMap](https://docs.rs/binemit/struct.StackMap.html))

Add stack map metadata for this program point: a set of stack offsets (from SP upward) that contain live references.

The `offset_to_fp` value is the offset from the nominal SP (at which the `stack_offsets`
are based) and the FP value. By subtracting `offset_to_fp` from each `stack_offsets`
element, one can obtain live-reference offsets from FP instead.

# MachTextSectionBuilder in cranelift_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-codegen/^0.106.2/struct.MachTextSectionBuilder.html

`pub struct MachTextSectionBuilder<I: VCodeInst> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Implementation of the `TextSectionBuilder` trait backed by `MachBuffer`.

Note that `MachBuffer` was primarily written for intra-function references
of jumps between basic blocks, but it’s also quite usable for entire text
sections and resolving references between functions themselves. This
builder interprets “blocks” as labeled functions for the purposes of
resolving labels internally in the buffer.

# VCodeConstants in cranelift_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-codegen/^0.106.2/struct.VCodeConstants.html

`pub struct VCodeConstants { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

This structure tracks the large constants used in VCode that will be emitted separately by the
[MachBuffer](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBuffer.html).

First, during the lowering phase, constants are inserted using [VCodeConstants.insert]; an intermediate handle, [VCodeConstant], tracks what constants are used in this phase. Some deduplication is performed, when possible, as constant values are inserted.

Secondly, during the emission phase, the [MachBuffer](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBuffer.html) assigns [MachLabel](https://docs.rs/struct.MachLabel.html)s for each of the
constants so that instructions can refer to the value’s memory location. The [MachBuffer](https://docs.rs/struct.MachBuffer.html)
then writes the constant values to the buffer.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# CodegenError in cranelift_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-codegen/^0.106.2/enum.CodegenError.html

```
pub enum CodegenError {
    Verifier(
```
[VerifierErrors](https://docs.rs/verifier/struct.VerifierErrors.html)),
    ImplLimitExceeded,
    CodeTooLarge,
    Unsupported([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    RegisterMappingError([RegisterMappingError](https://docs.rs/isa/unwind/systemv/enum.RegisterMappingError.html)),
    Regalloc([CheckerErrors](https://docs.rs/regalloc2/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/regalloc2/checker/struct.CheckerErrors.html)),
    Pcc([PccError](https://docs.rs/ir/pcc/enum.PccError.html)),
}## Expand description

A compilation error.

When Cranelift fails to compile a function, it will return one of these error codes.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Verifier)

### Verifier([VerifierErrors](https://docs.rs/verifier/struct.VerifierErrors.html))

A list of IR verifier errors.

This always represents a bug, either in the code that generated IR for Cranelift, or a bug in Cranelift itself.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ImplLimitExceeded)

### ImplLimitExceeded

An implementation limit was exceeded.

Cranelift can compile very large and complicated functions, but the [implementation has
limits](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/blob/main/cranelift/docs/ir.md#implementation-limits) that cause compilation to fail when they are exceeded.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CodeTooLarge)

### CodeTooLarge

The code size for the function is too large.

Different target ISAs may impose a limit on the size of a compiled function. If that limit is exceeded, compilation fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Unsupported)

### Unsupported([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

Something is not supported by the code generator. This might be an indication that a feature is used without explicitly enabling it, or that something is temporarily unsupported by a given target backend.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RegisterMappingError)

### RegisterMappingError([RegisterMappingError](https://docs.rs/isa/unwind/systemv/enum.RegisterMappingError.html))

A failure to map Cranelift register representation to a DWARF register representation.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Regalloc)

### Regalloc([CheckerErrors](https://docs.rs/regalloc2/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/regalloc2/checker/struct.CheckerErrors.html))

Register allocator internal error discovered by the symbolic checker.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Pcc)

### Pcc([PccError](https://docs.rs/ir/pcc/enum.PccError.html))

Proof-carrying-code validation error.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# RelocDistance in cranelift_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-codegen/^0.106.2/enum.RelocDistance.html

```
pub enum RelocDistance {
    Near,
    Far,
}
```
## Expand description

Notion of “relocation distance”. This gives an estimate of how far away a symbol will be from a reference.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Near)

### Near

Target of relocation is “nearby”. The threshold for this is fuzzy but should be interpreted
as approximately “within the compiled output of one module”; e.g., within AArch64’s +/-
128MB offset. If unsure, use `Far` instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Far)

### Far

Target of relocation could be anywhere in the address space.

This crate contains the control plane for "chaos mode". It can be used to inject pseudo-random perturbations into specific sections in the code while fuzzing. Its compilation is feature-gated to prevent any performance impact on release builds.

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/^1.3.1/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

# gimli 0.28.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/gimli/0.28.1

`gimli`

`gimli` is a library for reading and writing the
[DWARF debugging format](https://dwarfstd.org/).

-
**Zero copy:**everything is just a reference to the original input buffer. No copies of the input data get made.
-
**Lazy:**you can iterate compilation units without parsing their contents. Parse only as many debugging information entry (DIE) trees as you iterate over.`gimli`also uses`DW_AT_sibling`references to avoid parsing a DIE's children to find its next sibling, when possible.
-
**Cross-platform:**`gimli`makes no assumptions about what kind of object file you're working with. The flipside to that is that it's up to you to provide an ELF loader on Linux or Mach-O loader on macOS.- Unsure which object file parser to use? Try the cross-platform
`object``gimli-examples``gimli`.

- Unsure which object file parser to use? Try the cross-platform

## Install

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.28.1"
```
The minimum supported Rust version is:

- 1.60.0 for the `read`feature and its dependencies.
- 1.65.0 for other features.

## Documentation

-
Example programs:
-
`ddbug`
-
`dwprod``DW_AT_producer`).
-
`dwarf-validate`

# fallible_iterator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fallible-iterator/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

“Fallible” iterators.

The iterator APIs in the Rust standard library do not support iteration
that can fail in a first class manner. These iterators are typically modeled
as iterating over `Result<T, E>` values; for example, the `Lines` iterator
returns `io::Result<String>`s. When simply iterating over these types, the
value being iterated over must be unwrapped in some way before it can be
used:

In addition, many of the additional methods on the `Iterator` trait will
not behave properly in the presence of errors when working with these kinds
of iterators. For example, if one wanted to count the number of lines of
text in a `Read`er, this might be a way to go about it:

This will return the proper value when the reader operates successfully, but if it encounters an IO error, the result will either be slightly higher than expected if the error is transient, or it may run forever if the error is returned repeatedly!

In contrast, a fallible iterator is built around the concept that a call to
`next` can fail. The trait has an additional `Error` associated type in
addition to the `Item` type, and `next` returns `Result<Option<Self::Item>, Self::Error>` rather than `Option<Self::Item>`. Methods like `count` return
`Result`s as well.

This does mean that fallible iterators are incompatible with Rust’s `for`
loop syntax, but `while let` loops offer a similar level of ergonomics:

[§](https://docs.rs#fallible-closure-arguments)Fallible closure arguments

Like `Iterator`, many `FallibleIterator` methods take closures as arguments.
These use the same signatures as their `Iterator` counterparts, except that
`FallibleIterator` expects the closures to be fallible: they return
`Result<T, Self::Error>` instead of simply `T`.

For example, the standard library’s `Iterator::filter` adapter method
filters the underlying iterator according to a predicate provided by the
user, whose return type is `bool`. In `FallibleIterator::filter`, however,
the predicate returns `Result<bool, Self::Error>`:

```
let numbers = convert("100\n200\nfern\n400".lines().map(Ok::<&str, Box<Error>>));
let big_numbers = numbers.filter(|n| Ok(u64::from_str(n)? > 100));
assert!(big_numbers.count().is_err());
```

# indexmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/indexmap/^2.0.0/

## Expand description

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) is a hash table where the iteration order of the key-value
pairs is independent of the hash values of the keys.

[ IndexSet](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html) is a corresponding hash set using the same implementation and
with similar properties.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[are drop-in compatible with the std](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet``HashMap`
and `HashSet`, but they also have some features of note:- The ordering semantics (see their documentation for details)
- Sorting methods and the `.pop()`
- The `Equivalent`
- The `MutableKeys``MutableValues`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

To reduce the amount of compiled code in the crate by default, certain
features are gated behind [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section). These allow you to opt in to (or
out of) functionality. Below is a list of the features available in this
crate.

- `std`: Enables features which require the Rust standard library. For more information see the section on- `no_std`
- `rayon`: Enables parallel iteration and other parallel methods.
- `serde`: Adds implementations for- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `IndexMap`- `map::serde_seq`
- `arbitrary`: Adds implementations for the- `arbitrary::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`

*Note: only the  std feature is enabled by default.*

[§](https://docs.rs#alternate-hashers)Alternate Hashers

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[have a default hasher type](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet`[, just like the standard](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/hash/random/struct.RandomState.html)

`S = RandomState``HashMap` and `HashSet`, which is resistant to
HashDoS attacks but not the most performant. Type aliases can make it easier
to use alternate hashers:```
use fnv::FnvBuildHasher;
use indexmap::{IndexMap, IndexSet};
type FnvIndexMap<K, V> = IndexMap<K, V, FnvBuildHasher>;
type FnvIndexSet<T> = IndexSet<T, FnvBuildHasher>;
let std: IndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
let fnv: FnvIndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
assert_eq!(std, fnv);
```

# stable_deref_trait - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stable_deref_trait/^1.1.0/

## Expand description

This module defines an unsafe marker trait, StableDeref, for container types that deref to a fixed address which is valid even when the containing type is moved. For example, Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String implement this trait. Additionally, it defines CloneStableDeref for types like Rc where clones deref to the same address.

It is intended to be used by crates such as [owning_ref](https://crates.io/crates/owning_ref) and [rental](https://crates.io/crates/rental), as well as library authors who wish to make their code interoperable with such crates. For example, if you write a custom Vec type, you can implement StableDeref, and then users will be able to use your custom type together with owning_ref and rental.

no_std support can be enabled by disabling default features (specifically “std”). In this case, the trait will not be implemented for the std types mentioned above, but you can still use it for your own types.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Clone](https://docs.rs/trait.CloneStableDeref.html)- Stable - Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types where clones deref to the same address. This has all the requirements of StableDeref, and additionally requires that after calling clone(), both the old and new value deref to the same address. For example, Rc and Arc implement CloneStableDeref, but Box and Vec do not.
- [Stable](https://docs.rs/trait.StableDeref.html)- Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types that deref to a stable address, even when moved. For example, this is implemented by Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String, among others. Even when a Box is moved, the underlying storage remains at a fixed location.

# test_assembler - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/test-assembler/^0.1.3/

## Expand description

A set of types for building complex binary streams.

For testing code that consumes binary data, it is necessary to
be able to generate test inputs consisting of various valid and
invalid permutations. The `Section` struct defined in this crate
allows for easily building a stream of bytes in any desired
endianness.

This crate defines two useful structs: [ Section](https://docs.rs/struct.Section.html) and

[. A](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)

`Label``Section` is simply a stream of bytes which can
be written to, and a `Label` is a placeholder for a value that can be
computed based on other values, but can be written to a `Section` without
knowing its value at that time.This crate is based on [Jim Blandy’s fantastic C++ implementation](https://chromium.googlesource.com/breakpad/breakpad/+/master/src/common/test_assembler.h) in Google Breakpad.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

`Section` provides many convenient methods for appending data of specific endianness and byte width. There are methods for appending 8, 16, 32, and 64-bit integers using the `Section`’s default  endianness, or explicitly using big or little-endian byte ordering. These methods all have shorthand names of the form:

`[endianness][bits]`

Where `endianness` is one of:

- `D`: The- `Section`’s default endianness
- `L`: little-endian
- `B`: big-endian And- `bits`is any of 8, 16, 32, or 64 to write an integer from 1 to 8 bytes in length.

So, for example, to write a little-endian 32-bit integer, call [ L32](https://docs.rs/struct.Section.html#method.L32).

The `Section` methods for appending data all consume and return the `Section`
so that they can be chained:

```
use test_assembler::Section;
let mut section = Section::new();
assert_eq!(section.D8(0xFF).L16(0xABCD).B32(0x12345678)
            .get_contents().unwrap(),
           &[0xFF, 0xCD, 0xAB, 0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78]);
```
`Label`s can be appended to a section as placeholders for values that
are not yet known using the same methods:

```
use test_assembler::*;
let l = Label::new();
let mut s = Section::with_endian(Endian::Little);
s = s.D32(&l);
// Now assign a value to l.
l.set_const(0x12345678);
assert_eq!(s.get_contents().unwrap(),
           &[0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12]);
```
`Label`s can also be set to the current length of the `Section` by calling
[ mark](https://docs.rs/struct.Section.html#method.mark), which is useful for calculating an offset into the data:

```
use test_assembler::*;
let l = Label::new();
let s = Section::with_endian(Endian::Little);
let start = s.start();
s.append_repeated(0, 10)
    .mark(&l)
    .append_repeated(0, 10);
assert_eq!(&l - &start, 10);
```

# gimli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/gimli/latest/target-redirect/gimli/

## Expand description

`gimli` is a library for reading and writing the
[DWARF debugging format](https://dwarfstd.org/).

See the [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) and [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) modules
for examples and API documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

Cargo features that can be enabled with `gimli`:

-
`std`: Enabled by default. Use the`std`library. Disabling this feature allows using`gimli`in embedded environments that do not have access to`std`.
-
`read`: Enabled by default. Enables the`read`module. Use of`std`is optional. Requires the`alloc`crate.
-
`read-core`: Enabled by default. Enables a subset of the`read`module that does not require the`alloc`crate.
-
`endian-reader`: Enabled by default. Enables the`EndianReader``stable_deref_trait`crate.
-
`write`: Enabled by default. Enables the`write`module. Use of`std`is optional. Requires the`alloc`crate. Enabling both`read`and`write`will also enable conversion functionality in the`write`module.

- [Debug](https://docs.rs/struct.DebugTypeSignature.html)- Type - Signature
- A type signature as used in the `.debug_types`section.
- [Debug](https://docs.rs/struct.DebugTypesOffset.html)- Types - Offset
- An offset into the `.debug_types`section.
- [DwoId](https://docs.rs/struct.DwoId.html)
- An optionally-provided implementation-defined compilation unit ID to enable split DWARF and linking a split compilation unit back together.
- [EhFrame](https://docs.rs/struct.EhFrameOffset.html)- Offset
- An offset into the `.eh_frame`section.
- [Encoding](https://docs.rs/struct.Encoding.html)
- Encoding parameters that are commonly used for multiple DWARF sections.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineEncoding.html)- Encoding
- Encoding parameters for a line number program.
- [Little](https://docs.rs/struct.LittleEndian.html)- Endian
- Little endian byte order.
- [Location](https://docs.rs/struct.LocationListsOffset.html)- Lists - Offset
- An offset into either the `.debug_loc`section or the`.debug_loclists`section, depending on the version of the unit the offset was contained in.
- [Loong](https://docs.rs/struct.LoongArch.html)- Arch
- LoongArch architecture specific definitions.
- [MIPS](https://docs.rs/struct.MIPS.html)
- MIPS architecture specific definitions.
- [Power](https://docs.rs/struct.PowerPc64.html)- Pc64
- PowerPC 64bit
- [Range](https://docs.rs/struct.RangeListsOffset.html)- Lists - Offset
- An offset into either the `.debug_ranges`section or the`.debug_rnglists`section, depending on the version of the unit the offset was contained in.
- [RawRange](https://docs.rs/struct.RawRangeListsOffset.html)- Lists - Offset
- An offset into either the `.debug_ranges`section or the`.debug_rnglists`section, depending on the version of the unit the offset was contained in.
- [Register](https://docs.rs/struct.Register.html)
- A DWARF register number.
- [RiscV](https://docs.rs/struct.RiscV.html)
- RISC-V architecture specific definitions.
- [Unit](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitSectionOffset.html)- Section - Offset
- An offset into the `.debug_info`or`.debug_types`sections.
- [X86](https://docs.rs/struct.X86.html)
- Intel i386 architecture specific definitions.
- [X86_64](https://docs.rs/struct.X86_64.html)
- AMD64 architecture specific definitions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Dwarf](https://docs.rs/enum.DwarfFileType.html)- File - Type
- The “type” of file with DWARF debugging information. This determines, among other things, which files DWARF sections should be loaded from.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.Format.html)
- Whether the format of a compilation unit is 32- or 64-bit.
- [RunTime](https://docs.rs/enum.RunTimeEndian.html)- Endian
- Byte order that is selectable at runtime.
- [Section](https://docs.rs/enum.SectionId.html)- Id
- An identifier for a DWARF section.
- [Vendor](https://docs.rs/enum.Vendor.html)
- Which vendor extensions to support.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Clone](https://docs.rs/trait.CloneStableDeref.html)- Stable - Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types where clones deref to the same address. This has all the requirements of StableDeref, and additionally requires that after calling clone(), both the old and new value deref to the same address. For example, Rc and Arc implement CloneStableDeref, but Box and Vec do not.
- [Endianity](https://docs.rs/trait.Endianity.html)
- A trait describing the endianity of some buffer.
- [Stable](https://docs.rs/trait.StableDeref.html)- Deref
- An unsafe marker trait for types that deref to a stable address, even when moved. For example, this is implemented by Box, Vec, Rc, Arc and String, among others. Even when a Box is moved, the underlying storage remains at a fixed location.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [case_](https://docs.rs/fn.case_fold.html)- fold
- Perform case folding for the DWARF name index hashing.
- [case_](https://docs.rs/fn.case_folding_djb_hash.html)- folding_ - djb_ - hash
- Calculate a case folding DJB hash for the DWARF name index.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Native](https://docs.rs/type.NativeEndian.html)- Endian
- The native endianity for the target platform.
